problems.source_says: Figures 1 and 5 explicitly define each plotted observation as an original-draft/revised-draft pair linked by a semantic-change arrow. The codebook defines two outputs compared as unit='pair'; the 86 source essays therefore supply 86 D1-D2 pairs per revision condition. The same paired representation is already coded as 'pair' for its shift magnitude in S2-O2.
problems.quote: Each point pair represents an essay before (D1) and after (D2) revision
problems.locator: PDF p. 9, Figure 5 caption; p. 1, Figure 1 caption; p. 7, Section 3.2, PCA of Embedding Representations; creativity-codebook.md, Section 6, Unit.

confirmed: S1-O1 embeds each completed essay with MiniLM-L6-v2 and compares different writers' distributions using t-SNE; it is computed on outputs, not self-report or within-person flexibility (PDF pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2).

S1-O1 correctly uses diversity/across_people and output-level plotted points; its qualitative subgroup directions match the text, and no scalar diversity effect or inferential uncertainty is supplied (PDF pp. 8-9, Figure 4b and Section 4.2).

AI was available during S1 essay production in the assistance arm; no subsequent unassisted writing task was administered, so S1's other constructs use with_ai rather than after_ai (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 22, Appendices A.3-A.4; p. 24, Appendix A.6).

S1-O2 is a gpt-4o classification of each essay's stance, correctly treated as other/automated_score rather than creativity or diversity; all nine percentages, the 68.9% increase, t(69)=-2.439, p=0.017 and the prose bound p<0.036 match (PDF p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 10, Figure 6 and Section 4.3; p. 45, Appendix D.2).

S1-O3 classifies argument types present in each essay, not the number of distinct idea categories; expert-opinion t(69)=-2.78, p<0.01 and statistical-argument t(69)=4.82, p<0.0001 match Figure 10 (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 4.7 and Figure 10b; p. 45, Appendix D.2).

S1-O4 measures linguistic POS frequencies on essay text, correctly distinguished from creative flexibility; the reported 50% pronoun decrease, 14% noun increase and 33% adjective increase match the prose (PDF p. 11, Figure 8 left and Section 4.5).

S1-O5 is correctly marked scored_on_output=false and self_report at participant level: the question asks how creative participants felt while writing. Means 3.95/3.83/3.41 and t(69)=2.110, p=0.0385 match (PDF p. 24, Appendix A.6; p. 8, Figure 4a and Section 4.1).

S2 compares researchers' automated revisions with historical human revisions; its human writers did not receive the generated revisions as AI assistance, and this is not an after_ai task (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 3.1, ArgRewrite-v2; p. 26, Appendix B.1).

S2-O1's qualitative convergence interpretation is explicitly stated across essays from different students; the form correctly separates that interpretation from numerical within-essay shift magnitudes (PDF p. 1, Figure 1; pp. 7 and 9, Sections 3.2 and 4.2, Figure 5).

S2-O2 correctly uses pair and other for within-essay semantic change. Direct inspection of Figure 1 confirms Human 0.068, General 0.320, Minimal 0.315, Grammar 0.140, Completion 0.245 and Expansion 0.393, under gpt-5-mini with feedback (PDF p. 1, Figure 1 image and caption).

S2-O3 is unigram Jensen-Shannon divergence between original and revised drafts, not between-writer diversity; 0.476 for Claude general revision with expert feedback and the prose descriptions 0.2-0.3 and above 0.7 are correctly transcribed (PDF p. 7, Section 3.2; pp. 10-11, Section 4.4 and Figure 7).

S2-O4's POS categories and every recorded percentage/range match Section 4.5; they are identified as prose-reported changes relative to D1, not reconstructed AI-minus-human effects (PDF p. 11, Section 4.5 and Figure 8 right; pp. 38-42, Figures 31-35).

S2-O5 uses NRC emotion/sentiment word densities rather than creativity or diversity; the 37-54%, 17-53%, 24-38% ranges and human changes typically under 5% match the cited text (PDF p. 7, Section 3.2; p. 12, Figure 9 and Section 4.6; pp. 42-43, Figures 36-40).

S2-O6 is an output-level LIWC analytic-language score. Figure 10a's caption and visible Human D1/Human D2/gpt-5-mini labels support ArgRewrite-v2 despite the swapped dataset names in the prose; no exact group means are printed (PDF pp. 12-13, Section 4.7 and Figure 10a).
S2-O7 compares unique-word frequency profiles of human and model revision pools, supporting set/lexical_overlap/other rather than a between-writer diversity index (PDF p. 6, Figure 3).

S3-O1 and S3-O2 use gpt-4o to label review text with strengths and weaknesses; novelty labels concern the reviewed research, not the creativity of the review. The writing workflows are unobserved and AI source is detector-classified (PDF pp. 6-7, Sections 3.1-3.2; pp. 44-45, Appendix D.1).

All 85 numeric cells for S3-O1 and all 75 for S3-O2 match PDF Table 1 exactly, covering all 32 rows. The 18,000-review corpus count and the separate normalization by three possible labels per review are both explicitly reported and distinguished in the form (PDF p. 13, Figure 11; p. 46, Appendix E, Table 1).

The full markdown, including appendices and examples through p. 95, contains no additional reported output-scored creativity/diversity outcome or after_ai writing test missing from the form; self-reported voice and recommendation scores are already discussed in its notes (PDF pp. 8 and 14; pp. 22-26, Appendix A; pp. 43-46, Appendices C-E; pp. 47-95, Appendices F-I).
summary: S2-O1 miscodes the analysis unit as an output even though the plotted observations are paired original and revised drafts. Criterion 3 still holds because S1 computes cross-writer semantic comparisons on participants' completed essays.
